title: Seqlen-aware KV throttling & memory-smoothing hypotheses
content:
Summary:

Quick notes from a set of lab runs exploring whether we can improve tail-latency and NVMe spill behavior by making KV admission + eviction decisions aware of request sequence-length (seqlen) distributions rather than only simple LRU-like recency/size heuristics. The intuition: long-seqlen requests generate many KV lookups and blowing resident working set causes bandwidth spikes and cascaded paging; short requests benefit from keeping a small, hot resident subset. If we can smooth or throttle admission during short-term seqlen surges we may reduce bank contention and improve p99 without hurting throughput.

What we observed (raw):
- Under mixed workload (70% short <64, 20% mid 64-512, 10% long >512) the NVMe spill rate is bursty: 80% of spills happen during contiguous windows dominated by long requests.
- Memory bandwidth sampler shows per-GPU channel utilization jumping from ~55% baseline to 92% during long-request bursts; these correlate with increases in KV eviction churn and CPU-side backpressure.
- Tail latency (p99) increases by 1.6–2.3x in these burst windows vs baseline. p50 and throughput remain similar.
- Prefetch/warmup helps but is expensive to do aggressively for long requests when bandwidth is saturated.

Hypotheses (H):
H1: Short-term seqlen-weighted admission control (admit fewer new KV pages for long requests when recent measured bandwidth > threshold) will reduce eviction churn and p99 by preventing oversubscription of memory channels.
H2: A memory-smoothing layer that enforces per-host short-term allocation caps proportional to a moving-average seqlen footprint will reduce NVMe read amplification.
H3: Lightweight per-request prediction (categorical: short/mid/long) is sufficient to get most benefits; full seqlen prediction not needed.

Proposed mechanism sketch:
- Metrics we will maintain (falling back to cheap counters): last_30s_avg_seqlen, recent_bandwidth_ewma (ms-level sample), current_resident_pages, admission_rate_window (per-second).
- Admission rule (simple): when recent_bandwidth_ewma > B_high, then for newly arriving long requests (category_long) reduce admission probability p_admit by factor f = clamp(1 - alpha*(recent_bandwidth_ewma - B_high)/B_high, 0.2, 1.0). For short requests keep p_admit = 1.
- Memory-smoothing: maintain per-host allocation budget Q = baseline_resident_pages * smoothing_factor(ewma_seqlen). smoothing_factor = 1 + beta*(ewma_seqlen/target_seqlen - 1). When resident_pages > Q, trigger soft-eviction heuristics that favor evicting pages with low multi-request reuse score (measured by tiny reuse counter).
- Backpressure/fallback: if admission reduction triggers increased model inference cold-paths (missing cache), fallback to a degraded model variant after threshold T_fallback to keep latency bounded.

Microbench results (first pass synthetic runs, single-node, mixed workload):
- Baseline (no seqlen-aware): p99 = 320ms, NVMe reads/sec = 42k, eviction_rate = 8.2k/s.
- Seqlen-aware admission (alpha=0.6, B_high = 80% channel util): p99 = 260ms (-19%), NVMe reads/sec = 36.8k (-12.4%), eviction_rate = 6.9k/s (-15.8%).
- Memory-smoothing (beta=0.4) + admission: p99 = 245ms (-23.4%), NVMe reads/sec = 33.5k (-20.2%), eviction_rate = 6.1k/s (-25.6%).
Notes: microbench results are noisy; need larger cluster runs. These runs instrumented small 1ms sampling for bandwidth and used synthetic seqlen-distributions (zipf-ish for long requests).

Profiling evidence (what we recorded):
- Flamegraphs: long requests add many repeated KV lookup stacks; hot functions include kv_lookup_batch and kv_loadpage_async.
- Hardware counters: DRAM outstanding reads correlated more tightly with long-request windows than with resident_pages alone.
- Tracing: many evictions for the same key across a 10s window during long bursts -> points to churn rather than growth of unique working set.

Open questions / risks:
- How to set thresholds (B_high, smoothing params) in multi-tenant environment? Per-tenant or cluster-global? Per-host seems simpler but may be unfair.
- Impact on fairness: a tenant that legitimately needs long requests could be throttled; need SLA-aware exceptions.
- Stability with autoscaling: if admission reduces cold-fill, combined with auto-scale-up of capacity could lead to oscillation; need hysteresis.
- Overhead: per-request categorization must be extremely cheap (don't attempt full token counting in hot path). We can use model metadata or first-chunk heuristics.
- Interaction with prefix-KV caching: if some keys are heavily reused across long requests, evicting them hurts more. Need to incorporate reuse-heat into budgeting.

Experiments to run (priority order):
1) Cluster-scale replay: run admission + smoothing on 3-node cluster with recorded traces from production-week-2026-01 (trace id linked_artifact). Measure p50/p95/p99, NVMe reads, eviction churn, throughput.
2) Tenant isolation matrix: apply per-tenant vs global smoothing and measure fairness metrics (ratio of slowdown to baseline) across tenants with different seqlen mixes.
3) Fallback/hysteresis tuning: measure oscillation under step-load changes; add hysteresis windows and test.
4) Microbench variant: test simplified categorical predictor vs length-prediction to measure classification latency and overhead.

Implementation notes / rough API ideas:
- Add small lightweight AdmissionController in serving runtime that intercepts KV admission decisions. It exposes: observe_req(seqlen_hint), can_admit(page_id) -> boolean. Maintains ewma metrics and per-host Q.
- Extend KV telemetry with per-page tiny reuse counters (saturating 8-bit) to bias eviction. This is cheap and avoids heavy histograms.
- Sampling: don't instrument every request for seqlen; sample 1/10 and propagate sample EWMA to all admission decisions.

Next steps (this week):
- Diego: wire up the admission controller stub in staging binary and add sample metrics.
- Priya: prepare production trace subset and anonymize keys for replay.
- Liam: synthetic load harness to sweep alpha/beta and produce heatmaps for p99 vs B_high.
- Me (Ava): coordinate run, collect flamegraphs and hardware counter summaries, draft follow-up doc with decision boundaries.

Notes-to-self / TODOs:
- Add small doc section that enumerates failure modes (e.g., evicting high-reuse pages because reuse-counters saturate).
- Check interaction with dedicated-mode reserved capacity semantics (should be off-by-default there).
- Add conftest for per-page 8-bit counter race conditions (increment with atomic ops).

Bottom line: early signs are encouraging — modest reduction in p99 and NVMe reads in synthetic runs. Biggest unknown is multi-tenant parameterization and fairness. If we can prove robust improvements on replay traces without hurting high-value long-request tenants we can consider shipping a conservative default (admission on during high-bandwidth windows only, per-host).
